newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts urges quick tobacco settlement.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts urges quick tobacco settlement.

text.p: The Massachusetts attorney general Thursday urged Congress and President Clinton to quickly approve the settlement 42 attorneys general reached with the tobacco companies.

"There is a solid agreement here," Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger told reporters at his Boston office. "My next step is to join with other attorneys general in urging the president and Congress to review this in detail as quickly as possible...to avoid this becoming an issue of individual agendas and special interests.
"Let's get real here. It (the settlement) will not get tougher," he said.
He noted that each day "these issues languish without becoming the law the of land is another day that 3,000 more of our children will start smoking."

Harshbarger, expected to face Rep. Joseph Kennedy in next year's Democratic gubernatorial primary, took some shots at Congress in general, but declined to aim his pointed remarks at his probable opponent.

"The Congress of the United States could have and should have done many of these things years ago," Harshbarger said referring to the settlement's striction on advertising, ingredient disclosure and nicotine regulation.

Asked if he is prepared to defend the settlement, which some public health advocates have criticized as not going far enough, Harshbarger replied, "I am very glad to defend this negotiated settlement, our action in leading the fight against big tobacco against people who were missing in action and never been involved in the fight."

Under the settlement reached in June, the tobacco companies agreed to pay $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and accept extensive federal regulation over their products and their advertising as part of a landmark agreement. In return, the companies, would be given immunity from any further punitive liability for deception, fraud or conspiracy that might have occurred in the past.
